# Scope of this reference

This is one defensible solution, not the only acceptable one. The data are
synthetic, so the purpose is to make modelling decisions explicit: identifiers
are not measurements, nominal labels have no numerical order, and variable
importance is a choice to justify rather than a fact produced by software.

# 1. Data dictionary and distance specification

```{r import}
customers <- read_csv("data/customer_profiles.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    loyalty_tier = ordered(loyalty_tier, levels = c("Bronze", "Silver", "Gold", "Platinum")),
    preferred_channel = factor(preferred_channel),
    region = factor(region),
    uses_discount = factor(uses_discount, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

dictionary <- tibble(
  variable = names(customers),
  type = c("identifier", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "ordinal",
           "nominal", "nominal", "binary symmetric", "numeric count"),
  include_in_distance = c("No", rep("Yes", 8)),
  reason = c(
    "Labels rows only; numerical differences between IDs are meaningless.",
    "Range-scaled numeric difference.", "Range-scaled numeric difference.",
    "Range-scaled behavioural frequency.", "Ordered ranks are meaningful.",
    "Only same/different is meaningful.", "Only same/different is meaningful.",
    "Both Yes and No are informative here.", "Range-scaled behavioural count."
  )
)
knitr::kable(dictionary, row.names = FALSE, caption = "One defensible variable classification.")
```

The selected Gower dissimilarity is

\[
d_G(i,j)=
\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{p}w_k\,\delta_{ijk}\,d_{ijk}}
     {\sum_{k=1}^{p}w_k\,\delta_{ijk}}.
\]

For numeric variables, \(d_{ijk}=|x_{ik}-x_{jk}|/R_k\), where \(R_k\) is the
observed range. For nominal variables it is 0 for a match and 1 for a mismatch.
For an ordered factor it is the scaled rank difference. In this baseline all
weights are one; that is a transparent default, not proof that variables are
equally important for every business purpose.

```{r baseline-distance}
profiles <- customers |>
  select(age, income_k_eur, visits_last_month, loyalty_tier,
         preferred_channel, region, uses_discount, returns_last_year) |>
  as.data.frame()
rownames(profiles) <- customers$customer_id
d_gower <- daisy(profiles, metric = "gower")

pair_table <- function(d) {
  as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(d))) |>
    transmute(customer_1 = as.character(Var1), customer_2 = as.character(Var2),
              dissimilarity = Freq) |>
    filter(customer_1 < customer_2) |>
    arrange(dissimilarity)
}

pairs <- pair_table(d_gower)
pair_examples <- bind_rows(
  head(pairs, 3) |> mutate(comparison = "Closest"),
  tail(pairs, 3) |> mutate(comparison = "Most distant")
) |> select(comparison, customer_1, customer_2, dissimilarity)
knitr::kable(pair_examples, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Closest and most distant pairs for the equal-weight baseline.")
```

Close pairs should share several characteristics, not necessarily every one.
Conversely, a combination of different region, channel, discount use and
loyalty tier can make a pair distant even when ages are similar.

# 2. MDS map and its limitation

```{r baseline-map, fig.cap="Classical MDS of the equal-weight Gower dissimilarities. The axes are arbitrary coordinate directions, not customer traits."}
fit <- cmdscale(d_gower, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
map <- customers |>
  transmute(customer_id, loyalty_tier, preferred_channel,
            MDS1 = fit$points[, 1], MDS2 = fit$points[, 2])

ggplot(map, aes(MDS1, MDS2, colour = loyalty_tier, shape = preferred_channel,
                label = customer_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(nudge_y = .025, show.legend = FALSE, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Customer profiles under equal-weight Gower dissimilarity",
       colour = "Loyalty tier", shape = "Preferred channel")

map_distance <- dist(fit$points)
cor(as.vector(d_gower), as.vector(map_distance))
```

The map gives a compact view of major profile contrasts. It is not complete:
Gower dissimilarity is not guaranteed to be Euclidean, and two dimensions cannot
preserve every pairwise distance. The correlation printed above is a descriptive
diagnostic of distance reproduction, not an acceptance threshold.

# 3. Why arbitrary numeric codes are not valid

If Mobile = 1, Store = 2 and Web = 3, Euclidean distance says that Mobile is
twice as far from Web as it is from Store. Replacing the codes with Mobile = 1,
Store = 3 and Web = 2 reverses that geometry without changing the observed
categories. The numerical gaps come from the coding decision, not the data.
A nominal variable should enter through a same/different comparison.

# 4. Homework extension

## 4.1 Give recent visits double weight

```{r weighted-distance}
weight_visits <- c(age = 1, income_k_eur = 1, visits_last_month = 2,
                   loyalty_tier = 1, preferred_channel = 1, region = 1,
                   uses_discount = 1, returns_last_year = 1)
d_weighted <- daisy(profiles, metric = "gower", weights = weight_visits)

knitr::kable(head(pair_table(d_weighted), 6), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Closest pairs after giving visits double weight.")
```

The weighting is defensible only if visit frequency is genuinely twice as
important for the stated segmentation purpose. It must be documented and checked
as a sensitivity analysis; choosing weights merely because they create a desired
visual grouping is not defensible.

## 4.2 Remove age and income

```{r remove-demographics, fig.cap="Removing age and income changes the target from demographic-plus-behavioural similarity to engagement and preference similarity."}
profiles_behavioural <- profiles |> select(-age, -income_k_eur)
d_behavioural <- daisy(profiles_behavioural, metric = "gower")
fit_behavioural <- cmdscale(d_behavioural, k = 2)

behavioural_map <- customers |>
  transmute(customer_id, loyalty_tier, preferred_channel,
            MDS1 = fit_behavioural[, 1], MDS2 = fit_behavioural[, 2])
ggplot(behavioural_map, aes(MDS1, MDS2, colour = loyalty_tier,
                            shape = preferred_channel, label = customer_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(nudge_y = .025, show.legend = FALSE, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Profiles after removing age and income",
       colour = "Loyalty tier", shape = "Preferred channel")
```

Removing variables changes the scientific question; it is not merely a graphical
adjustment. This version compares engagement, loyalty and preferences rather
than a broader demographic-plus-behavioural profile.

## 4.3 Distance-reproduction plot

```{r shepard, fig.cap="Pairs far from the diagonal are poorly reproduced by the two-dimensional map."}
original <- as.matrix(d_gower)
mapped <- as.matrix(map_distance)
reproduction <- tibble(
  customer_1 = rownames(original)[row(original)[upper.tri(original)]],
  customer_2 = colnames(original)[col(original)[upper.tri(original)]],
  original_distance = original[upper.tri(original)],
  map_distance = mapped[upper.tri(mapped)]
) |> mutate(absolute_error = abs(original_distance - map_distance))

ggplot(reproduction, aes(original_distance, map_distance)) +
  geom_point(colour = blue, alpha = .7) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = orange, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Original Gower dissimilarity versus map distance",
       x = "Gower dissimilarity", y = "Two-dimensional MDS distance")

knitr::kable(slice_max(reproduction, absolute_error, n = 1),
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Pair with the largest distance-reproduction error.")
```

The pair with the largest error deserves inspection, but it is not necessarily
an error in the data. It is a relationship that cannot be retained faithfully in
this two-dimensional representation.

# 5. Example decision memo

> We compared anonymised customer profiles, excluding the identifier. We used
> Gower dissimilarity because the variables include numeric measures, an ordinal
> loyalty tier, nominal channel and region, and binary discount use. Numeric
> differences were scaled by observed ranges and baseline weights were one.
> Classical MDS gives an exploratory map in which nearby points have similar
> profiles under this explicit specification. The axes are not customer traits,
> and the map does not reproduce every dissimilarity exactly. Any weighting must
> be tied to a documented purpose. Customer profiling can also amplify unfair
> treatment or support inferences beyond the data, so the map is not an automated
> decision rule.
